Name: Soham Mehta
Question: To those of you who interviewed for a software engineering role at Google, Facebook, Amazon and got in without preparing for the interview, will you share your experience?
Answer: Context and disclaimer: I run an intense and successful bootcamp focused on preparing for Tech interviews. A 100+ people from all over the world have prepped with us since we started a year and a half ago: http://interviewkickstart.com We've since learnt a lot about what makes successful engineers. While nearly everyone who goes thru us (and is actively looking) gets placed somewhere nice, the people who crack some of the hardest interviews generally fall into ONE or MORE of the following categories: 1. They are just bright from the get go. A high IQ. These are your friends who you have always wondered how easily they "get" things. They come up with keen observations the fastest. They can get by with normal amount of practice viz. brush-up. Not saying they are the happiest people on the planet, but they often don't need the kind of prep you and I do. 2. They are extremely prepped. Extremely. A crude measure of prep, is how many data-structures/algorithmic problems you've practiced. Some of these people have crossed 300+ problems. Written code for each. And repeated it. It takes several months to a year to do this with diligence and focus. 3. They have been coding for a long time. Almost precocious-ly. They have written so much code, that a lot of constructs are now muscle memory. All they need to do in an interview, is to intuit the solution. After that, they impress the heck with their coding fluency. 4. They are competitive programmers for some time. They don't have to be toppers or winning competitions. e.g. Yellow on Topcoder is sufficient. 5. They went to a particularly strong and competitive CS program Some programs in the country prepare you for such interviews. Rare, and difficult to get into, but they do. 6. They got a soft interview-panel. Interviews are heavily dependent on who interviews you. At large companies, there is a wide variance in grading standard, experience in interviewing and in beliefs, and hence there is a wide variation in intake bar, despite centralized hiring committees. You need a bit of luck anyway, but sometimes you get an entire panel that you happen to gel with. A little bit of preparation and getting such a panel puts you over the magic line. Lesson? Prepare. You'll be glad you did. Not because it just might get you a ticket to some of the best gravy trains on the planet, but because the right kind of interview preparation actually makes you a better engineer in your daily work.

Question: If there is such a high demand for tech positions, why don't they pay more?
Answer: You are kidding, right? Let’s try to see this from a more objective high level and paint some broad strokes: Take a look at this official source of US Govt data: Computer and Information Technology Occupations The median income for someone with an associate’s degree, is 66k+. Median income. i.e. half of income earners at that level, make more than 66k per year, just after 2 years of post-highschool education, if that. Here is more: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (Occupation Finder). Like any other profession, Tech also has a pyramid of skills+talent, where higher you are, the more you get paid. e.g. if someone hires you to create a key-value store for their company from scratch, you’re going to be paid more than if someone hires you to silence Nagios alerts. HOWEVER, today Tech is one of the few industries (or maybe the only?) where ALL of the following are true, AT THE SAME TIME: Now, $60K could seem less. But know that $60K puts you into middle-class, just after two years in college. Very few professions in very few countries of the world can claim that. And the compensation grows rapidly from there. In order to ascend to higher levels of the pyramid, you need to remain up-to-date on newer, in-demand skills and target to work at some of the best tech companies. It’s amazing what a few months of preparation can do.

Answer: Summary: Lots of people from our Coding Interview Bootcamp have done exactly this. We have a lot of first-hand data. A lot of this is dependent on what stage of life you are in. Like I’ve quoted Coach Paul Bryant before: Everyone wants to win (in this case, get higher salary), but very few want to prepare to win. You seem to be the latter kind of engineer. So, welcome to my world and hear me out! (No, not about smoking, but the greenback :-)). We have helped many candidates from Coding Interview Bootcamp negotiate compensation. And obviously, by definition, not everyone gets to or even wants to optimize careers for high pay. Question: How common is $300k total compensation for Silicon Valley engineers?
Answer: Strictly speaking, it’s not “common”, but more achievable than many software engineers believe. Most engineers don’t even try sincerely, which is unfortunate. Engineers making this kind of money in the Bay Area, work at “top-tier” tech companies. What is “top tier” is fuzzy: It includes companies big and small, new and old, core tech and not. What’s common to all these companies, is that they value technical talent very highly. They are willing to open up their wallets for better talent, because they believe that better talent leads to faster growth (and it often does). By definition, such “top tier” tech companies are few, maybe 20%. If you’re a job-seeker, then probably the real question you’re asking, is how does one get such comp? Here is the blueprint: Not saying it’s easy to do, but never in the history of the world, has there been a clear path to riches in such abundance (thousands of such engineering openings at any given time in the valley), like it is now. A few months of hard work, a lifetime of gravy.

Question: What are the best-kept secrets about startups?
Answer: Your success is more dependent on your skills in messaging, than it's on access to money or strategy. Your initial customers will come because they believe in you and your vision. That comes when you can effectively communicate what you offer. Your initial hires are also going to come because they believe in your and your vision. They are going to be inspired by what you say and how you say it. Your investors are going to be the same. Your acquisition is dependent on how you've presented yourself in the industry, which in turn depends on what you say and how you say it. Once you start on an idea you're passionate about, you'll notice that you'll need to experiment with how to explain it properly. It can take several tries, and often months, to get to a narrative that generally works. If you can get to a narrative that works reliably with just a certain kind of audience (one distribution channel), then that is the first turning point of your business. It's not about marketing blasts on facebook; it's about nailing one distribution channel with precise messaging. Having the runway and perseverance to survive until you cycle through different distribution channels, and nail that narrative with one, with a high-enough conversion rate (even 10% is great), is the difference between really getting off the ground, and not. In fact, despite iterating several times, if you are finding it difficult to nail your messaging for a given audience, that may be your earliest indication that product-market fit is going to be very difficult. Messaging is that powerful secret, in plain sight.
